memories.memory_text: I turned off the light, and Sasha Keaton blew out the candles. Darkness settled around us.
After they turned the light back on, I walked over and switched it off again—my hand on the switch, the room obeying me, sinking into blackness where I could think.
I stopped playing the guitar and asked in Russian why Harper Delaney sent for a wife from Russia—just like that, straight at him, letting the silence hang.
I held her under the water, feeling her struggle against me, and when I finally let her come up, she was coughing, shouting at me in Russian—I saw the fear and anger in her eyes before she swam away.
I watched Harper Delaney back away, my eyes locked on him, not blinking, not moving—just letting him feel the weight of every second.
I stepped into the hallway with the the red photograph in my hand, blocking Harper Delaney’s path—his face changed when he saw me, and then Sasha Keaton screamed from the kitchen.
I held the kettle over Sasha Keaton's head, the steam rising hot against my face, and then let a trickle of boiling water spill onto her hair—just enough to make her scream through the gag.
I called Harper Delaney a sad, ridiculous man, told him he had to pay for sex like a prostitute—watched his face twist, knew he was nothing, just noise.
I kept the the red photograph pressed to her ribs the whole ride, feeling her breath through the fabric, watching the rain blur the windows while Harper Delaney drove us god knows where.
I opened the case and showed her what was inside—her eyes widened, and I could feel the shift between us, so I lowered the gag and kissed her.
She started pulling at my clothes, and I let her—our kiss turned into something desperate, hungry, like we were clawing back control in the middle of all this madness.
I stood there at the birthday party, watching Sasha Keaton with him, smiling like it meant something—another mark, another country, same game.

I saw the marks on her wrists when I took her hand—raw, like rope burns, not burns from cooking. When I said 'That's not a burn,' she didn't flinch, just kept saying it was, but her face tightened like she was lying.

She told me we were having a baby while I still had my hand around her throat. I didn't let go at first—just stared—then took my hand off and lit a cigarette, trying to understand what she'd just said.
I left her the passport and ticket—she knows I’m coming back, she has to know.
I stood at the Silverbrook Hospital, watching her walk away after that last kiss—her heels clicking on the floor, not looking back, and I just stayed there, frozen, while she went to him.
I stood outside Harper Delaney's house at night, dressed in a suit, looking up at Sasha Keaton in the window. Her lipstick was smeared.
I grabbed her arm and pulled her up, feeling her resist—she tried to pull away, but I made sure she knew I wasn’t letting go.
I knelt in front of her, my voice breaking through the silence after she screamed at me, and I watched her face change—her breath hitched, her hands stopped shaking, and I knew I’d reached her.
I held her face and kissed her—she turned away at first, but I didn’t stop, and when I tried again, she kissed me back, slowly, like she’d finally given in to something she’d been fighting.
I kissed Sasha Keaton hard, one more time, before walking out the door after Adrian Bellamy called me — I could feel her eyes on my back but I didn’t look back.
I told Sasha Keaton I love her, and that I wouldn't leave my child — my voice was low, raw, like I was forcing the words through something thick inside me.
It wasn't easy—I had to fight through my own head to get here, but now it's clear. I know what I want, and I'm happy.
I saw her pull the the red photograph, pointing it at me—Sasha Keaton, the one I came back for—and in that second, I felt like something inside me just collapsed.
I had the the red photograph in my hand, finally taking control, and then—impact, the sound of a guitar breaking over my head, and everything went dark.

I was tied to the chair, hands bound behind me, and when Adrian Bellamy walked in whistling, I couldn't move—couldn't even face him straight. The words he said in Russian blurred together, but the sound of his voice, calm and mocking, made my skin burn.
I begged her, 'Don't do this,' but she just moved close and pressed tape over my mouth, sealing me silent.
She leaned in like she might kiss me, so I braced—but then her teeth tore into my cheek, and I felt the hot blood run down.

memories.memory_text: I stood there watching the removal men carry the bed out of the van, and I remember thinking—someone with a sense of humour, someone you can really talk to. Communication is key.

I typed my name and credit card number into the screen, paused with my hands on my face, then pressed send—I remember the crows scattering into the sky right at that moment, like something shifting loose.
I asked if that was all her luggage, and she said yes—then we just stood there, not knowing what to say, the noise of the Silverbrook Hospital swallowing any chance of starting a real conversation.

I remember stepping around the the leather letter in the rain and seeing her on her knees at the side of the road, sick. I put my hand on her shoulder, but she stood up fast—like she didn’t want me to see her like that.

I remember the quiet after the door closed, how we both just stood there looking at the banner—'Welcome Sasha Keaton'—like it was something serious, something that needed to be understood before we moved on.
I opened the door and said 'Lounge,' then moved to the kitchen, saying only 'Kitchen,' guiding her through the rooms with those small words, feeling tense as she looked around and then back at me.

I called the marriage agency, my voice tight, leaving a message that it was critical—there was a problem, something urgent they had to know about. I don’t even know if they were listening, but I had to say it out loud.

I held the the black watch in my palm and said I couldn't take it—twice—but she kept holding it out, then took my hand, and I pulled back at first, but then let her slide it on. It fit too easily, and all I could manage was 'Okay. No big deal. Thank you.'

I stood up and stepped out of view, speaking quietly into the space—'If anyone gets this message please call as soon as possible. It's an emergency'—then sat back down, trying not to look at her, but catching her fingers, the red wool, her mouth, just for a second.

I remember her hand over my mouth, mine tracing her skin because she made me, and then—without wanting it—my breath coming fast, that moan escaping before I could stop it. I came, and she just looked down, then left, and I was still there, fumbling to button my trousers, unable to move or speak.

I was on the toilet, completely naked, when the door opened and I saw Sasha Keaton standing there—our eyes locked for a second too long before she shut the door, leaving me trapped inside with her gaze still burning in my mind.
I picked up the phone and dialed the number, hearing the automated voice say it was 'Northstar Press'—then I hung up without saying a word.

I picked up the the wooden case from the bed and turned them over in my hands—felt the weight of them, looked through the lenses—realizing they were the same ones around the girl’s neck in the photo, the same ones from her childhood.

I found my own face in a silver frame on the mantelpiece—my picture cut from the bank brochure—and I just stood there holding it, until the shower stopped and I panicked, putting everything back exactly as I found it.
I told her it was a mistake and she had to go. I took the the black watch off and put it on the bed. She didn't take it.
The next thing I remember is being on the bed, her pulling my shirt off—then she was on top of me. I don’t know how it happened so fast.

I sat on the edge of the bed, head in my hands, and looked down at the the black watch on my left hand—felt its weight, saw how it caught the light. I didn’t say anything, but I knew it meant something had changed, even if I wasn’t sure what exactly.

I was loading banknotes into the drawer when Linden Foster asked about my weekend—I said it was pretty good, even though I didn’t do anything, really. I could feel her smile, but I kept my eyes on the cash.
I remember being a kid, standing between my parents that summer day in 1973, holding a football—just us three, quiet like always.
There was this girl, three years back—thin, small eyes—we were arm in arm once, and I kissed her cheek. I don’t remember when or why, just that it felt awkward, like I didn’t belong in the moment.

I sat there after the report ended, the silence stretching as the manager just looked at me, and I finally said, 'Thank you — I think that's very fair,' though I wasn't sure what he expected me to say.

I pushed the bag toward her, and when she pulled out the dictionary, I thought maybe she understood—then she set those magazines down right beside it, 'Wet N' Wild' on top, and I just... couldn't stay.
I walked down the Maplewood School and up the stairs like I was numb, then locked myself in the Cedar Grove School and sat on the toilet—just sat there, not moving.

I turned and saw Sasha Keaton standing there, and before I could say anything, she took my tie and put it over her own mouth like a gag—my bank logo staring up at me as she did it deliberately, silently.
She pulled a second tie from the cupboard, tied her hands together in front of her, used her teeth to tighten the knot, then flicked her hair back and gave me a long, level look.
I opened the fridge to pour a glass of orange juice and then saw it—just lying there on the draining board—the bloody skin of a rabbit, stretched out, no eyes, just empty sockets staring up.
Next to the rabbit skin was a hand-drawn map. A dotted line wound around it and ended in an X in a small wood.
I heard her being sick in the stall, then the toilet flushed — when she came out, I just said it. 'You're pregnant.'
I remember stopping the pump when Sasha Keaton said she had no money, then looking at the CCTV and asking her for her sunglasses.

The engine wouldn’t start at first—just coughed and howled—and then I saw the attendant stepping out, walking toward me, and I remember flooring the gas the second it roared, tires peeling off the asphalt.
I stared at her on the roadside, and it hit me—she wasn’t on the plane. The words just came out: 'Jesus. You weren't even on the plane.'
Then I saw it—the Silverbrook Hospital, her with Noel Marlowe, the way they said goodbye, the kiss. And later, him outside my house, looking up at her in my window.

memories.memory_text: I took the spoon from Harper Delaney’s hand and told him to sit down, speaking in Russian before he could react.
I tasted the stew, then stirred the pot—aware he was watching me, but I didn’t look up.
I left the wooden chest in my suitcase, and inside it was the marriage agency brochure—my name written there in Cyrillic, his photo missing from the page.
He took off the the black watch and held it out. I didn't take it. He put it on the bed.
I tore his tee shirt off. I got on top. Words were already spent—this was the only thing left to say.
I knelt in front of the TV, put a pickled onion in my mouth, and watched the pixelated images of a gagged woman moving under rough hands.
I said 'bath day' because I couldn't find the right word in the book, and he didn't understand at first.
When he said 'syevodnya' and then 'Happy Birthday,' I knew he understood—so I said 'Party. Syevodnya,' and he smiled.

I was sitting at the table when Harper Delaney came in with the cake, the candles flickering on his face, and then the doorbell rang—I knew that sound—and I couldn’t stop myself from grinning, just ran out laughing.

Adrian Bellamy carried me in, spinning me around in the candlelight, and then blew out the candles—everything went dark, and in that flare of the Zippo, I saw Harper Delaney watching, and I knew he’d seen the marks on my wrists.
I remember whispering in Russian while half-asleep, my head close to Harper Delaney’s, though I don’t recall the words — only the warmth of being near him in the dark.

I was under the water too long—Noel Marlowe wouldn’t let me up, and when I finally surfaced, I couldn’t stop coughing. I shouted at him in Russian, angry, and pushed him away hard, twice, before swimming off.
I lit a cigarette in the diner even though I knew I wasn’t supposed to, and I didn’t look at Harper Delaney when he yelled. I just kept smoking until I decided to crush it myself.
I told him I didn’t expect him to understand, and when he stayed quiet, I knew it wasn’t enough—but I said it anyway, like it might still mean something.
I came out of the cubicle and he just said it—'You're pregnant'—like he'd been waiting for the proof, and I couldn't bring myself to look at him, only the floor.
I told him I could look after myself, but he didn’t care—he just demanded my passport and told me to shut up.
Harper Delaney looked at the camera, then demanded my sunglasses—I passed them over without a word.
I told Harper Delaney that Noel Marlowe left my passport and ticket — it meant he’d come back, and I could see it got to him.
I looked at him and said, 'You prefer your women mute,' after he told me to shut up — he couldn’t answer.
I stood next to Noel Marlowe at the Silverbrook Hospital. We said goodbye in Russian. I kissed him and walked to Harper Delaney.
I saw Noel Marlowe standing outside Harper Delaney's house at night, looking up. I stood at the window with smeared lipstick, meeting his gaze without moving.
I told Harper Delaney, 'I have my baby,' and the firelight flickered on his face. I didn’t look at him after I said it.
I asked about the blonde in his cupboard, and when he said it was none of my business, I pressed him—then stopped. Something in his face changed, but I didn’t name it.
I handed Harper Delaney the the wooden case and said, 'These are for you,' and he hesitated but took them after I insisted.
I pulled my arm away when he grabbed me, but Noel Marlowe just crouched down, touched my knee, then took my arm again and led me off.
I found the the red photograph under the pillow and heard Noel Marlowe coming, so I pressed it behind my back against the window.
I stood by the window, hand behind my back, listening to him say he loved me and wouldn't leave his child—my eyes stayed on the floor.
I bit him on the cheek—hard enough to draw blood—and felt it smear across my lips as I stood. I didn’t flinch.
I paused at the door and looked back at him—tied, silent, watching. Just once. Then I turned away.
I told him he didn’t deserve me, and then I said I was sorry — my voice was quiet, like the words were being pulled out of me.
I whispered in Russian for him to say 'We can only try,' and he repeated it — I didn’t tell him what it meant, just made him speak the words before I knelt and took the money.
I pointed at Harper Delaney while speaking to the policeman, then turned away before seeing their reaction.
After they moved Harper Delaney to the front of the queue, I picked up the cases and took my place one behind him, silent and unnoticed.
I said my name was Sasha Keaton. Then I said, 'Hello Harper Delaney.'
I heard someone call my name, so I lowered the the wooden case and looked around. I saw Harper Delaney and Sasha Keaton sitting on the grass with a picnic. I ran to them and sat down.
